title: If intelligence becomes a commodity, what stays scarce?
summary: As Anthropic's record IPO and a Fed warning put AI economics in focus, we ask what stays scarce when intelligence becomes a commodity. Read our analysis of where the value goes.
body_markdown:
Anthropic’s record IPO this month raised about $81 billion at a fully diluted valuation of approximately $1.5 trillion. But the most revealing numbers sit behind the headline. Its prospectus describes roughly $901 billion in purchase and lease commitments, substantially all related to compute and infrastructure. Those obligations extend as far as 2045, with approximately $71 billion due in the twelve months following September 2026. They are long-term commitments, not a single immediate debt bill. They nevertheless show the scale of investment required to stay at the right at the frontier.¹


The filing also makes the dependencies clear. Some infrastructure providers rely on third-party financing or credit support to deliver capacity. If that support becomes unavailable (Jenson’s handshake is the new loan officer) or more expensive (Fed hiking), even contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced or reduced. A company raising capital on this scale still depends on the economics of the infrastructure around it.¹


November’s market debate has repeatedly returned to those economics. In a speech in Milan, Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr compared the growth of AI-related borrowing with the telecom investment cycle of the late 1990s. He distinguished potential direct credit losses from the danger of a reversal that forces investors to deleverage and sell. He also highlighted a fundamental difference between the assets being financed: power connections may remain useful for decades, while specialised chips can lose value quickly.²


That distinction matters to investors. AI can transform the economy while some of the companies financing its expansion earn disappointing returns.


It is also the question behind


[The Great Diffusion](https://coinshares.com/insights/research-data/the-great-diffusion/)


, the investment thesis CoinShares published this week.


## Cheap intelligence <> cheap infrastructure


Our starting point is that more AI capability is becoming available at lower prices. Open-weight models are narrowing the gap (6 months behind) with leading closed models, making a growing range of commercial tasks accessible without paying for the most advanced system.


That does not mean the leading labs will fail. Better models can command a premium, particularly where small improvements in performance have substantial economic value. Reliability, security, integration and customer relationships matter too. Falling prices per task can also coexist with growing revenue and profits if usage expands sufficiently.


Our question is how much pricing power a technological lead can sustain as cheaper alternatives become good enough for more of the work customers need.


If that pricing power weakens, some of the value may accrue elsewhere: to the companies applying AI effectively, and to the owners of resources that remain difficult to reproduce. Our research examines electricity, advanced silicon, settlement infrastructure, proof of authenticity and neutral reserve assets.


But scarcity alone does not make a good investment. The question is whether it lasts long enough to earn a return after the cost of building, financing and replacing the asset.


## The lesson from telecom


The telecom boom demonstrated how technological progress and investment returns can diverge. Companies financed and built networks that helped enable the internet economy. Some failed financially even as the infrastructure they created became increasingly useful.


AI infrastructure deserves the same scrutiny. We need to distinguish between an asset that remains scarce and one whose current price simply reflects a temporary shortage. We also need to ask who captures the benefit when capacity becomes cheaper: the infrastructure owner, the customer or the end user.


A grid connection, a data centre and a GPU are all part of the AI buildout. They have different useful lives, replacement costs and exposure to technological change. Treating them as one investment theme obscures the risks.


## Where crypto fits


I see three distinct opportunities worth examining.


-


Opportunity 1: The rails - settling payments between machines


In


[October](https://coinshares.com/insights/the-node/output-the-dollar-went-on-chain-the-euro-went-to-committee/)


, I wrote about machines buying computation from machines. If those transactions grow across platforms and jurisdictions, open settlement networks could offer advantages in availability, programmability and interoperability. That is an argument for examining the infrastructure. It is not, by itself, an argument for buying its token. A network can process more transactions without passing meaningful economic value to token holders. We need to establish who pays, who receives the fees and what rights an investor actually owns.


-


Opportunity 2: The power - turning energy access into revenue


The second opportunity is already visible in listed markets. Some bitcoin mining companies hold power contracts, energised sites and grid connections that AI developers need. Those assets can create commercial opportunities.The assessment must remain specific to each company and site. A mining facility is not automatically suitable for AI workloads. Conversion costs, financing, customer contracts and delivery timelines determine whether the opportunity produces an attractive return. The scarcity premium may also diminish as new capacity arrives.


-


Opportunity 3: The compute - building a market for processing capacity


The third is computing capacity becoming a more standardised, tradable exposure. GPU rental-price benchmarks already exist, and CME Group has announced plans for futures linked to H100 and B200 rental indices. These are financially settled contracts linked to rental prices, rather than ownership of the underlying hardware.³


Decentralised networks are pursuing another approach, using tokens to encourage suppliers to provide computing resources. They may identify a real market, but their economics need to stand on their own.


The test is straightforward: can payments from genuine customers cover the full cost of supplying the service, including hardware depreciation, electricity and operations, without relying on newly issued tokens?


Subsidies can help a network get started. They do not establish that it has a sustainable cost advantage. We should distinguish a low price funded by incentives from one made possible by greater efficiency.


Bitcoin’s potential role as a neutral reserve asset is a separate argument. It rests on whether investors and economic participants value an asset that no single state issues. Growth in AI or machine payments would not, on its own, prove that investment case.


## What would change my mind


We have set out tests and a timetable in the paper because an investment thesis should explain what would invalidate it.


I would reconsider the commoditisation premise if leading open-weight models fell more than nine months behind closed models for two consecutive quarters, or if the leading labs demonstrated durable pricing power at comparable capability levels. A sustained failure of the cost of inference at constant quality to fall by at least half over twelve months would also challenge our assumptions.


The decentralised-compute argument has its own test. By the end of 2027, I would like to see evidence that genuine customer demand can support the service without continuing token subsidies. If that evidence is absent, I would drop that part of the investment case. It would not invalidate every other conclusion in the paper.


There are several ways to be right about the importance of AI and still lose money investing in it. Paying too much, financing the wrong asset or owning a token with no reliable claim on the value created are three of them.


AI can transform the economy without rewarding every company financing its expansion. Our job is to distinguish technological progress from investment returns and to show investors where the two can meet.
